summary.summary: Brent's 2024/25 outturn shows external borrowing up £85.8m (10.5%) to £900.0m, funding a capital programme that pushed the Loan CFR up £102.6m to £1,357.1m (General Fund £1,015.1m, HRA £342.0m). A £13.7m budget variance on capital financing costs (£41.5m actual against a £27.8m budget) was offset by a drawdown from capital reserves. The council has grown related-party lending to its wholly-owned housing companies — £182.4m to I4B Holdings Ltd and £33.8m to First Wave Housing — and holds £59.5m of LOBO loans, of which £35.0m face an interest-rate review in 2025/26.

signals.headline: External borrowing rose £85.8m (10.5%) to £900.0m in 2024/25, from £170.0m of new loans against £84.2m of repayments.
signals.why: A rapid, double-digit rise in the debt stock within a single year.

signals.headline: A £13.7m capital-financing budget variance (£41.5m actual vs £27.8m budget) was offset by drawing down capital reserves.
signals.why: Financing costs are already outrunning budget, absorbed by reserves rather than a revised budget.

signals.headline: £35.0m of the council's £59.5m LOBO book (5 loans) is due an interest-rate review in 2025/26.
signals.why: If a lender exercises its option the council's own option is to repay at par, which is what councils do: every LOBO call we hold — Kent, Tameside, Newcastle, York, Barnet, Brighton and Hove, Bristol — was repaid rather than accepted. So the exposure is finding £35.0m and replacing that funding at today's rates, not paying a higher rate on it.

signals.headline: Loans to Brent's wholly-owned companies stood at £182.4m to I4B Holdings Ltd and £33.8m to First Wave Housing at 31 March 2025, both secured on company property, plus a £36.4m equity stake in I4B.
signals.why: Sizeable related-party credit exposure sits alongside the headline treasury debt figures.

news_drafts.headline: Brent's £39.5m of LOBO loans include a £9.5m loan with an option date in December 2026
news_drafts.lead:
Brent Council holds £39.5m of LOBO loans, and one of them, for £9.5m, reaches an option date in December 2026, according to its mid-year treasury management report for 2026/27. A LOBO loan is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. The report, for the Audit and Standards Advisory Committee meeting of 30 November, does not say what will happen at that date.

The debt and investment appendix puts the LOBO loans at an average rate of 3.00% at 30 September 2026. They are one of six external borrowing lines, alongside £443.7m of equal instalment principal loans and £415.9m of maturity loans from the Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils. Total external debt stood at £1,081.1m at that date, with net debt of £1,007.5m.

The council's liability benchmark, a chart councils must publish comparing the debt they hold with the debt they actually need, forecasts the LOBO balance falling from £59.5m in 2025/26 (actual) to £39.5m in 2026/27, then £30.0m in 2027/28, £15.0m in 2028/29, £10.0m in 2029/30 and nil by 2030/31. The paper says the council uses the option date as the maturity date for its LOBO loans. It says the council will keep the LOBO portfolio under review and consider opportunities to repay or restructure.

news_drafts.headline: Brent forecasts £20.8m schools-grant overspend for 2026/27, taking its deficit to about £41m
news_drafts.lead:
Brent forecasts a £20.8m overspend on its dedicated schools grant (DSG, the government grant that funds schools) for 2026/27, which the council's papers say would take the cumulative deficit to approximately £41m by 31 March 2027. The forecast, as at 26 September, sits almost entirely in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities: £104.9m of spending against £84.1m of funding. The total adds the £20.2m deficit brought forward from 2025/26.

The budget had already planned a £14.9m overspend in high needs. The paper says the high needs allocation "did not increase at all" in 2026/27, while the number of education, health and care plans, the legal documents setting out a child's support, rose by 10.4% as of January 2026.

Brent submitted its SEND Reform Plan in June 2026 and has recently been told it is accepted for the High Needs Sustainability grant, which the paper says will cover 90% of the deficit to March 2026. The statutory override, a government rule that lets councils keep such a deficit off their main balance sheet, has been extended to March 2028. The paper says deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28 have no confirmed funding, and that the Government has not said what funding will follow after 2028/29.

The first two phases of the council's SEND capital programme are expected to add over 594 specialist places by January 2030.
news_drafts.paper_title: 08. Update on DSG HNB and Brent's SEND Reform Plan

news_drafts.headline: Brent pension fund reports 113% funding level at 2025 valuation, up from 87% in 2022
news_drafts.lead:
Brent's pension fund is in surplus, with a funding level of 113% at its 2025 valuation, against 87% at the 2022 valuation. The figure appears in the risk register presented to the council's Pension Board on 5 November 2026.

The register reports the whole-fund valuation results, which were presented to the Pension Fund Sub-Committee in October 2025. It says: "the Brent Fund now maintains a 113% funding level and is in surplus, compared to 87% in the 2022 valuation". A funding level compares the fund's assets with the cost of the pensions it has promised to pay.

The paper also records that the fund's prudence level on the key discount rate assumption was increased to 80%. The discount rate is the rate used to turn future pension payments into a value today. The papers give no further detail on the surplus or on what it means for contributions.

findings.headline: The Capital Expenditure (Hybrid) follow-up records its actions as implemented; the original review was rated Moderate and listed 22 agreed actions.
findings.detail: The paper records the follow-up status as actions recorded as implemented. The original review had four Medium-risk findings and three Low-risk findings, with 14 Medium and eight Low agreed actions.
findings.matters: Capital expenditure controls are the controls behind capital programme delivery and borrowing needs, which other councils and lenders track closely.
findings.figures: 22 agreed actions (0 High, 14 Medium, 8 Low); 4 Medium and 3 Low original findings
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure (Hybrid) Moderate Hybrid follow-up – actions recorded as implemented

findings.headline: Budget Pressures / Savings Delivery is a Priority 2 area in internal audit's Q4 risk assessment, covering the realism of savings and forecast accuracy.
findings.detail: The proposed scope covers governance, monitoring and delivery of key savings and pressure areas, along with realism of savings, forecast accuracy and corrective action. The paper says the list is fluid and subject to change.
findings.matters: Whether savings are realistic and forecasts accurate is a question a finance director at any council, and any lender, will ask of the budget.
findings.quote: Governance, monitoring and delivery of key savings and pressure areas, realism of savings, forecast accuracy and corrective action.

findings.headline: Commercial property leases and rent collection is a Priority 1 area for internal audit's Q4 work, with the paper describing the commercial estate as a key income stream.
findings.detail: The proposed scope covers lease management, rent invoicing, arrears monitoring, data accuracy, rent reviews and governance for maximising income. The paper names economic volatility and arrears risk as the exposures.
findings.matters: Commercial estate income and arrears are a source of revenue pressure that finance directors and lenders are tracking across councils.
findings.quote: The commercial estate is a key income stream exposed to economic volatility and arrears risk.

findings.headline: The paper reports that KPI6, which targets 75% of audit actions implemented within original timescales, is partially met.
findings.detail: The paper says the population of follow-ups completed so far in 2026-27 is limited, though the trend appears to be on track. KPI4 (acceptance of recommendations) and KPI5 (follow-up of Critical and High-risk actions within one month of due date) are recorded as met.
findings.matters: The on-time implementation rate is a measure of whether the council's own remediation deadlines are being kept, which other councils will compare against.
findings.figures: Target 75% of audit actions implemented within original timescales; 100% target for acceptance of recommendations met
findings.quote: There is a limited population size for follow-ups completed thus far in 2026-27, though trends appears to be on track.

findings.headline: Nine audit reviews list outstanding High-risk actions, with Health & Safety (22) and Property Assets and Valuations (14) having the largest counts.
findings.detail: For each review, the paper gives the latest original implementation date and the revised date set by management. Direct Payments to Children has six High-risk actions, with the original date of 31 July 2025 revised to 30 November 2026. The paper notes that revised deadlines do not indicate actions have been implemented.
findings.matters: A consolidated list of revised deadlines across multiple services shows where the council has moved its own targets, which peers will want to track for their own remediation plans.
findings.figures: Health & Safety 22 High actions; Property Assets and Valuations 14 High actions; Direct Payments to Children 6 High actions (original date 31 July 2025, revised 30 November 2026)
findings.quote: Actions remain outstanding pending Internal Audit verification.
